subtopics.title: Push and Pull: The Engine of Rural–Urban Migration

questions.question: A push factor in rural–urban migration is:
options: A condition at home that drives people away, such as unemployment or failing services
An attraction of the city, such as higher wages
A law forcing people to move
The cost of the taxi to town

questions.question: The phrase 'real or believed' matters in describing pull factors because:
options: Cities publish false statistics deliberately
Migrants often move on the perception of opportunity, and the city does not always deliver
Pull factors are always imaginary
Push factors are stronger than pull factors

questions.question: Rural–urban migration is selective in that it mostly moves:
options: The elderly and the very young
Entire villages at once
Young, economically active adults — historically men first, through the migrant labour system
Only professional workers

questions.question: Rural depopulation is defined as:
options: The seasonal movement of farm workers
The growth of informal settlements in cities
The forced removal of rural communities
The decline of the population living in rural areas as out-migration outruns natural increase

questions.question: A structural cause of rural depopulation, beyond the standard push factors, is:
options: Mechanisation and consolidation of commercial farms, replacing workers with machines
Higher rural birth rates
Urban housing shortages
Improved rural clinics

questions.question: The population pyramid of a depopulating village is 'pinched at the waist' because:
options: Birth rates have collapsed to zero
The working-age middle has left, leaving children, the elderly and mostly women
The census misses rural households
Death rates are highest among teenagers

questions.question: A balanced evaluation of out-migration notes that it also brings:
options: Higher rural land prices
More learners into village schools
Remittances sent home, eased pressure on communal land, and returning migrants with skills and savings
Guaranteed jobs for those who remain

subtopics.title: Strategies, Social Justice and Access to Resources

questions.question: The test of a good anti-depopulation strategy is whether it:
options: Increases the urban housing supply
Switches off a specific push factor, so home offers a living
Bans people from moving to cities
Raises the price of taxi fares

questions.question: Agri-processing plants fight depopulation by:
options: Creating jobs where people live, adding value to local produce instead of railing it away raw
Mechanising the remaining farms faster
Reducing the need for rural roads
Replacing small farmers with corporations

questions.question: The Natives Land Act of 1913:
options: Established the first land restitution courts
Distributed farmland equally among all South Africans
Abolished traditional authority over communal land
Restricted black land ownership to a small fraction of the country

questions.question: Depopulation runs hardest in the former homeland districts because:
options: Their climates are the wettest in the country
Large populations were concentrated on the least productive land with the least investment in infrastructure
They lie closest to the coast
Their populations were always the smallest

questions.question: Land tenure reform:
options: Moves families onto newly purchased farms
Returns land taken in the forced removals
Strengthens the rights of people already on the land, protecting them from arbitrary eviction
Nationalises all commercial farmland

questions.question: Land redistribution differs from restitution because redistribution:
options: Faces forward — transferring farmland for equity and livelihoods without a claim to one specific historical farm
Requires proof of a removal after 1913
Only compensates people in money
Applies only to communal land

questions.question: A valid restitution claim requires:
options: Proof of farming skills and a business plan
Dispossession of specific land after 19 June 1913 by racially discriminatory laws
Current residence on commercial farmland
A willing seller in the district

questions.question: Land reform doubles as a depopulation strategy because:
options: It forces migrants to return home
It closes urban informal settlements
It reduces the rural birth rate
Secure rights on productive land provide a livelihood at home — what migration promises, without leaving

questions.question: In the kitchen-table story, the aunt in Durban with a room available is:
options: A pull factor — family ahead offering a first bed and first contact
A push factor driving the school leaver out
A structural cause of depopulation
A land reform beneficiary

questions.question: The 'rumour the city spreads' refers to:
options: Radio advertisements for urban housing
News of relatives who failed in town
The perception of jobs and wages that the city does not always deliver
Official migration statistics

questions.question: Migration happens, in the lesson's terms, when:
options: The government offers transport
The shove of push factors plus the tug of pull factors outweighs the comfort of staying
The harvest is especially good
The whole family can move together

subtopics.title: The Village After the Taxi Leaves

questions.question: Rural depopulation is compared to a slow puncture because:
options: It happens in a single dramatic event
It only affects transport
It repairs itself over time
There is no single bang — the village just loses a little more every week as closures trigger departures

questions.question: The new brick rooms rising beside old rondavels are visible evidence of:
options: Remittances — wages sent home by family members working in the cities
Government housing programmes
Rising local farm incomes
Tourism revenue

questions.question: The closure of a village school often leads to:
options: More families moving in for the open space
Further departures, which trigger the next closure — the self-feeding spiral
The reopening of the bank branch
An immediate rise in local wages

questions.question: The single test for any anti-depopulation strategy in the lesson is:
options: How much the strategy costs
Whether the city approves of it
Which push factor does this switch off?
How many tourists it attracts

subtopics.title: Three Repairs for One Old Injustice

questions.question: The three-generation farm family who can be evicted by one letter is repaired by:
options: Redistribution — buying them a different farm
Restitution — returning land taken elsewhere
Tenure reform — strengthening their right to remain where they already are
A social grant

questions.question: The scene of a district where farmland belongs to a handful of owners calls for:
options: Redistribution — assisting new owners to buy and farm the land for equity going forward
Tenure reform for the existing owners
A restitution claim by the municipality
Consolidating the farms further

questions.question: The community pointing at a fence saying 'our families were removed from THIS land after 1913' is pursuing:
options: Tenure reform
Redistribution
A willing-seller purchase
Restitution — a named place, a proven removal, a return or a payout

questions.question: The three verbs that keep the legs of land reform apart are:
options: Buy, sell, lease
Strengthen, share, return
Plough, plant, harvest
Move, merge, mechanise
